sentences.text: Adult Thescelosaurus measured roughly 3 to 4 meters in length and weighed between 200 and 300 kilograms.
The largest known Thescelosaurus species, T. garbanii, was estimated to be 4 to 4.5 meters long and weigh between 200 and 300 kilograms.
Thescelosaurus possessed a long, low snout that terminated in a toothless beak.
Thescelosaurus had a very long tail that constituted half of its total body length.
Skin impressions from a 2022-discovered Tanis specimen show that parts of Thescelosaurus were covered in scales.
A Thescelosaurus specimen unearthed in 1999 was once thought to contain a fossilized heart, but this identification is now doubted by scientists.
In 2000, researchers interpreted a chest concretion in the "Willo" specimen as a fossilized heart with three low-density areas resembling ventricles and an aorta.
A 2022 documentary reported that a Thescelosaurus specimen supposedly died on the day of the K-Pg extinction, covered in skin impressions including long scales on its legs.
Paul Barrett noted that the skin impressions indicate Thescelosaurus was not feathered, unlike other small neornithischians.
One specimen of Thescelosaurus had fused long bones in the right foot, a pathology that likely hindered rapid movement.
A near-complete skeleton of Thescelosaurus was discovered in July 1891 by John Bell Hatcher and William H. Utterback along Doegie Creek in Wyoming.
William Parks described the species T. warreni in 1926 based on a skeleton found in the Edmonton Formation of Alberta, Canada.
Thescelosaurus was an herbivore that likely fed selectively based on its specialized teeth and narrow snout.
Thescelosaurus was likely a herbivore, similar to other ornithischian dinosaurs.
Its sharp beak and front teeth suggest it could have consumed some animal material.
Thescelosaurus had robust limbs with a femur longer than its tibia, suggesting it was not adapted for running.
In 1915, Gilmore proposed that Thescelosaurus was an agile, two-legged animal adapted for running.
Thescelosaurus had a small brain similar in size to ceratopsids like Triceratops, suggesting cognitive abilities within the range of modern reptiles.
The hypothesis that Thescelosaurus rib plates were armor for defense was refuted because Sharpey's fibers indicate they were embedded in muscle rather than being osteoderms.
A 2011 unbiased census study estimated that Thescelosaurus made up 8% of the dinosaur fauna in the Hell Creek Formation.

Researchers suggest that the disproportional presence of Thescelosaurus fossils in sandstone compared to ceratopsians in mudstone might indicate a preference for habitats along channel margins rather than floodplains.
Morris paid attention to deeply inserted premaxillary tooth rows, interpreting them as support for the presence of muscular cheeks.
Thescelosaurus likely browsed low to the ground, feeding selectively while holding food in its cheeks while chewing.
The genus Bugenasaura was once considered a synonym of Thescelosaurus but is now rejected.
Thescelosaurus is the namesake genus of the family Thescelosauridae.
The name Bugenasaura combines the Latin words for large cheek and the Greek word for lizard.
Charles Gilmore initially classified Thescelosaurus as a member of the family Camptosauridae in 1913.
Thescelosaurids are debated as being either basal ornithopods or placed outside the ornithopod group within Neornithischia.
Thescelosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the late Maastrichtian age.
Thescelosaurus lived around 66 million years ago, making it one of the last non-avian dinosaurs before the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.
Thescelosaurus lived in western North America during the late Maastrichtian age, approximately 66.04 million years ago, just before the extinction event.
Specimen AMNH 5034 was found just 5 feet below the Fort Union Formation, representing the youngest locality where dinosaurs have been found.
William J. Morris suggested that T. edmontonensis and T. garbanii might be separated from Thescelosaurus as a new genus, arguing their ankle anatomy was distinct from T. neglectus.
It is debated whether the hindlimb of T. garbanii actually belongs to the pachycephalosaurid Stygimoloch instead.
The assignment of most Thescelosaurus specimens to specific species remained uncertain because overlapping bone material for direct comparison was often unavailable.
